cultivar: Anshun Zhuyeqing and other medium- and small-leaf types
processing: A green tea from local medium- and small-leaf bushes, combining traditional handling with modern technology.
harvest_season: Exact picking calendars are little documented; as with other Guizhou greens, spring leaf is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Tight, even strips with a glossy grey-green colour.
appearance_wet: Even green leaf, as is typical of well-picked Guizhou greens.
taste_profile: Full and fresh with a high, lasting aroma and a long sweet finish.

brewing.notes: General advice for Guizhou greens: water around 85 C, and do not over-steep the fuller strip styles.

vintage_note: Sold as green tea, so the current year's harvest is what to look for, and spring lots are the usual premium, as with other Chinese greens. Producers sell it in named grades such as Yuya and Yufeng rather than by year.
description:
Duobei tea comes from Huachu town in Puding county, Anshun, in western Guizhou, where the Duobei area sits around 1,100 to 1,300 metres. It is one of Guizhou's traditional tribute teas and now a protected regional name.

Its calling card is the old bushes. Huachu keeps a stock of native tea plants estimated at over a hundred years old, some said to be far older. A shrub on the tribute hill at Zhangjiazhai village was assessed in 2008 as more than a thousand years old, and a tree named Chongzhen No. 1 is put at nearly 400 years.

The tea itself is made as a green tea with tight, even strips and a grey-green sheen. The cup is full and fresh with a strong aroma and a long sweetness. Keep the water a bit below boiling to hold on to that.

The protected area covers eleven townships of Puding county, so the name by itself does not mean old-bush leaf. Ask what the tea is actually picked from. Producers also use grade names like Duobei Yuya and Duobei Yufeng, and they also make a ginkgo tea that is a different drink.
history:
The Puding county gazetteer records a tradition that Duobei tea served as tribute in the Ming dynasty. The Anshun prefecture gazetteer gives a firmer date, placing tribute to the court in the Chongzhen years (1628 to 1644). The place name is said to have changed over time from an older written form, 多贝, meaning many treasures in the ground.

The tea was sent to a national agricultural show in Beijing in 1958, and in 1960 Puding county officials presented it to Zhou Enlai when he passed through Guiyang.

Its modern brand dates from provincial tea policy in 2007. Geographical indication protection followed on 21 February 2013, and in 2020 the tea was included in the first China and EU list of protected names.
